newsitem.title: INDIA: India says pushing ahead with missile programme.
newsitem.headline: India says pushing ahead with missile programme.

text.p: India, wedged between nuclear-armed China and nuclear-capable Pakistan, is pressing ahead with a controversial indigenous missile programme in the face of international pressure, the Defence Ministry said.

In the absence of any movement towards universal nuclear disarmament, New Delhi also plans to retain the option to build nuclear arms, the ministry said in its report for the year ending March 31, 1997, obtained by Reuters on Sunday.

"As with India's nuclear capability, it has also had occasionally to withstand international pressures brought to bear on its missile programme. The indigenous development of missile capability by India is in response to the evolving security environment in its region," the report said.
The United States and other countries have opposed India's missile programme, which Washington says could upset regional stability.
India has successfully tested the 250-km (150-mile) surface-to-surface Prithvi missile, a 150-km (90-mile) variation, the anti-tank Nag missile and a multi-barrel rocket launcher, Pinaka, it said.

New Delhi has also successfully tested the medium-range surface-to-air Akash missile and the quick reaction short-range Trishul missile, and completed trials of Akash self-propelled launchers, the Defence Ministry says.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda last month threw his weight behind a programme to indigenously develop the intermediate range Agni missile, a 2,500-km (1,500-mile) missile believed capable of carrying a nuclear warhead.
The Agni was mothballed last December due to what defence analysts said was U.S.-led opposition to India's missile programme, which Washington says could upset regional stability.

The longer-range missile is seen as a potential deterrent to China while the Prithvi is considered more suited as a deterrent against neighbouring Pakistan, which is suspected of having the ability to quickly assemble nuclear weapons.
This is the first time that the ministry's annual report has identified China's nuclear weapons and missile programmes as a significant Indian security concern, defence analysts say.
A decades-old military relationship between China and Pakistan, which says it has achieved nuclear capability without conducting a single test, has often stoked regional tensions.

Both Pakistan and China deny a series of Western reports that Beijing transferred to Islamabad nuclear weapons components and Chinese M-11 missiles that can deliver nuclear warheads. But India views their close ties with considerable concern.
China and India fought a brief border war in 1962. Indian analysts say China's first nuclear test just two years later prompted India's only nuclear test in 1974.
Pakistan and India, which have gone to war three times since 1947, say they have no nuclear arms but experts say either can assemble them swiftly.

The report said the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme had slowed during the year, partly due to fresh curbs on technology imports imposed by an international pact known as the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR).

"In order to ensure that Trishul, Akash and Nag systems are developed in the shortest possible time, the existing linkages with national science and technology resources have been strengthened further and the projects are being closely monitored," it added.
India says agreements like the MTCR are discriminatory.
"Those who have been seeking to impose restraints on India have in the meanwhile themselves continued their nuclear weapons and missile research programmes," the report said.

India last year refused to endorse a treaty banning nuclear test explosions, saying it was not a disarmament measure and would allow the declared nuclear powers to refine their arsenals through laboratory tests.
New Delhi also opposes a proposed pact banning materials used to make nuclear weapons unless it was linked to disarmament, the report said.
